changes.after: Record a change automatically, but skip assignments that keep the same value.

before: A trigger is database work that runs automatically when its specified event happens. Unlike a SELECT, it can cause additional writes.
The supplied database has notes(id,title) and note_audit(note_id,old_title,new_title). Titles are never NULL in this fixture.
In an UPDATE trigger, OLD refers to the row before the update and NEW refers to the row after it. OLD.title and NEW.title read those two title values.
AFTER means the row update happens before this trigger’s work. UPDATE OF title identifies updates assigning that column, even when the assigned value equals the old value.
WHEN NEW.title <> OLD.title limits the trigger to changed titles. The <> operator means not equal. Use NEW.id for the note identity.
The supplied operations change note 1 from Moon to Moon draft, leave note 2 at Sea, then change note 1 to Moon final. The audit should contain exactly the two actual changes, in their recorded order.
Use the isolated practice data only. Triggers run inside database operations and their effects participate in transactions; test them before applying them to real stored data.
after: A trigger is saved database work that runs automatically when a chosen event happens. Here, updating a label can add a row to a change log.
A change log stores what a value was before and after a change. The exercise has `notes` for the current titles and `note_audit` for the change records.
Inside an update trigger, `OLD` means the row before the update. `NEW` means the row after it. `OLD.title` and `NEW.title` read those two versions of the title.
`AFTER UPDATE OF label` chooses assignments to the label column. `AFTER` runs the trigger's work after the row update. An assignment can happen even when the value stays the same.

`<>` means not equal. The `WHEN` condition allows the log entry only when old and new values differ. This comparison works for the supplied titles, which are never `NULL`. If missing values are allowed, the comparison needs to handle them too.

Name your trigger `record_title_change`. Store `NEW.id`, `OLD.title`, and `NEW.title` in `note_audit`. The supplied updates make two real title changes and one unchanged assignment, so the log needs two rows.
The trigger's writes belong to the same transaction as the update. Rolling back that transaction also undoes its log entries.

before.question: An UPDATE assigns the same title it already had. Why is the WHEN comparison needed in this trigger?
choices: UPDATE OF can fire for that assignment even though the title value did not change.
AFTER triggers never see the previous value.
The comparison makes unchanged data disappear.
before.explanation: The event identifies the update operation; the condition separately decides whether the value actually differs.

after.question: An update assigns the same title again. Why does the trigger need its WHEN condition?
choices: The update event can happen even when the value stays the same
AFTER triggers cannot read the old value
after.explanation: The event tells us an assignment happened. The condition checks whether the value actually changed.

project.title: Record only real title changes
project.task: Create `record_title_change`, an `AFTER UPDATE OF title` trigger on `notes`. When the old and new titles differ, add the note ID and both titles to `note_audit`. Run the supplied updates.
project.done_when: The checks pass, and the log contains exactly the two real changes with no row for the unchanged title.
